street_smart.title: You're withdrawing cash at an ATM late in the evening. The card slot looks slightly loose and a stranger nearby offers to 'help' when your card seems stuck. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Evergreen rotation topic (credit/debit card skimming) — no single matching incident in today's feeds, and this topic hasn't appeared in the last three weeks. Chosen to pair with today's news of a Bengaluru woman losing ₹45 lakh to financial fraud, keeping the day's practical theme on money safety.
street_smart.situation: Your card doesn't come out right away, the machine screen looks slightly different from usual, and a stranger standing nearby steps in offering to enter your PIN or jiggle the card out for you.

choices.text: Refuse the stranger's help, cover the keypad while you try your PIN once more yourself, and if the card still doesn't come out, leave without re-entering your PIN and immediately call your bank's helpline to block the card.
choices.feedback: Correct. A loose-looking slot and a stuck card are classic signs of a skimmer or a card-trapping device. Never let a stranger touch your card or see your PIN, and blocking the card immediately cuts off any window for the fraudster to use a cloned copy.

choices.text: Let the stranger enter your PIN since they seem to know how to fix stuck cards.
choices.feedback: This is the trap: 'helpful stranger at a jammed ATM' is a well-known skimming and shoulder-surfing setup — either they capture your PIN by watching or typing it themselves, or they're working with a skimmer already fitted inside the slot. Never let anyone else touch your card or keypad, no matter how confident they sound.

choices.text: Walk away and forget about it, planning to deal with the card later.
choices.feedback: If the card was actually captured by a trapping device or skimmed, every hour you wait is an hour a cloned card or captured PIN can be used. Report and block the card the same day, don't wait.

choices.text: Try entering your PIN two more times to force the card out.
choices.feedback: Repeated PIN entry on a compromised or malfunctioning machine risks your card getting blocked by your bank's own fraud system, or worse, feeds a skimmer more attempts to capture your PIN. Stop after one retry and call your bank instead.

takeaways: Before inserting your card, check if the card slot looks loose, add-on, or different in colour/texture from the rest of the machine — that's the most common sign of a skimmer.
Never let a stranger touch your card or watch you enter your PIN at an ATM, however helpful they seem.
If your card is retained or you suspect tampering, call your bank's 24x7 helpline immediately to block it rather than waiting till the next day.
